title: What is a tree?
intro: Folders on your computer, a family tree, a tournament bracket: all of them are trees. In this lesson you'll learn the words used to describe them.

blocks.html: A tree stores data in a hierarchy. Each item is a node, and the lines that join nodes are edges. A tree never has a loop: there is exactly one path between any two nodes.

blocks.caption: A tree with 7 nodes and 6 edges.

blocks.html: Think of your Documents folder. It holds sub-folders, which hold more folders and files. That is a tree.

items: Root: the single node at the top (50 above).
Parent and child: 30 is the parent of 20 and 40; they are its children.
Leaf: a node with no children (20, 40, 60 and 80).
Subtree: a node together with everything below it.
Level (depth): how many edges a node is from the root. The root is at level 0.
Height: the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf. The tree above has height 2.

blocks.html: In a binary tree, every node has at most two children, called the left and right child. Every tree in this app is a binary tree.
A node can have zero, one or two children. "Binary" sets a maximum, not an exact number.

points: A tree is made of nodes joined by edges, with no loops.
The top node is the root. Nodes with no children are leaves.
Height is the number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.
In a binary tree, every node has at most two children: left and right.

title: Binary search trees
intro: Imagine a library catalogue where every book has a number. A binary search tree (BST) arranges those numbers so you can find any book with only a few checks.

blocks.html: For every node: all values in its left subtree are smaller, and all values in its right subtree are larger.

blocks.caption: Everything left of 50 is smaller than 50; everything right of it is larger.

blocks.html: The rule applies to the whole subtree, not just the direct children. 45 could never sit in 50's right subtree.
Start at the root. If the value you want is smaller, go left; if it is larger, go right. Stop when you find it, or when you fall off the tree.
To insert a value, search for it. The empty spot where the search falls off the tree is exactly where the new node goes.

blocks.text:
insert 35:  35 < 50 → left
            35 > 30 → right
            35 < 40 → left (empty) → place 35 here

blocks.html: Each comparison throws away about half of the tree, so a balanced BST with n nodes needs about log₂ n checks: 10 checks for 1,000 books.
Insert values that are already sorted, though, and every node goes to the right. The tree becomes a long chain and search slows to O(n).

blocks.caption: Inserting 10, 20, 30, 40 in order gives a lopsided tree.

points: BST rule: everything in a node's left subtree is smaller; everything in its right subtree is larger.
Search: compare with the node, go left if smaller, right if larger. Each step throws away half the tree.
Insert: search for the value; where you fall off the tree is where it goes.
A balanced tree searches in O(log n). Inserting sorted values makes a lopsided tree that searches in O(n).

title: Breadth-first search (BFS)
intro: The library robot has to check every shelf in the catalogue tree, starting at the top. Breadth-first search does it level by level: the whole top shelf, then every shelf one level down, and so on. By the end you'll be able to list the BFS order of any tree.

blocks.html: A traversal visits every node in a tree exactly once. BFS is one way to choose the order: visit every node on one level, left to right, before moving down to the next level.

blocks.caption: BFS visits level 0 (50), then level 1 (30, 70), then level 2 (20, 40, 60, 80).

blocks.html: BFS order for this tree: 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. Read the tree like a page of text: top row first, left to right.
To keep track of which node comes next, BFS uses a queue: first in, first out (FIFO). Nodes join at the back and leave from the front.

items: While the queue is not empty, take the node at the front and visit it.
Add that node's left child, then its right child, to the back of the queue (if they exist).
Repeat until the queue is empty.

blocks.html: Why a queue? Children join behind everything already waiting, so every node on the current level leaves the queue before any node on the next level.
Step forwards and watch the queue on the right. Each step takes one node from the front and adds its children to the back.

blocks.caption: A tree with 6 nodes. 65 has only a left child.

blocks.html: Look at step 2: 15 and 35 join the queue behind 65. That is why 65 is visited before them, even though they were added later.

items: BFS finds the node closest to the root first, such as the nearest damaged shelf.
On graphs, BFS finds the shortest path (fewest edges) between two points, for example in route planning or social networks.
BFS prints a tree level by level.
Every node is visited once, so BFS takes O(n) time. The queue holds at most about one level of the tree.

points: A traversal visits every node exactly once.
BFS visits the tree level by level, left to right.
BFS uses a queue (first in, first out): take a node from the front, visit it, add its children to the back.
BFS finds the node closest to the root first, and shortest paths on graphs. It runs in O(n) time.
